'''''Pinguicula vulgaris''''', the '''common butterwort''', is a [[perennial]] [[carnivorous plant]] in the [[butterwort]] genus of the family [[Lentibulariaceae]].

==Description==
It grows to a height of {{convert|3–16|cm}}, and is topped with a purple, and occasionally white, flower that is {{convert|15|mm}} or longer, and shaped like a funnel. This butterwort grows in damp environments such as bogs and swamps, in low or subalpine elevations.<ref>''Plants of the Pacific Northwest''. Lone Pine Publishing, 1994. p. 351</ref> Being native to environments with cold winters, they produce a winter-resting bud ([[Hibernaculum (botany)|hibernaculum]]). There are three forms originating from Europe: ''P. vulgaris'' f. ''bicolor,'' which has petals that are white and purple; ''P. vulgaris'' f. ''albida,'' which has all white petals; and ''P. vulgaris'' f. ''alpicola,'' which has larger flowers.<ref>''The Savage Garden, Revised: Cultivating Carnivorous Plants''. Random House LLC, 2013.</ref> The taxonomic status of these forms is not universally recognised – see e.g. The Plant List.<ref name=TPL>{{cite web |url=http://www.theplantlist.org/tpl1.1/record/kew-2537397 |title=The Plant List (2013). Version 1.1.: ''Pinguicula vulgaris'' L. |publisher=Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew and Missouri Botanic Garden |location=London, U.K. |accessdate=2 September 2016 }}</ref>

Common butterwort is an insectivorous plant. Its leaves have glands that excrete a sticky fluid that traps insects; the glands also produce enzymes that digest the insects.<ref name=CBSnews>{{cite news |title= Nature up close: The carnivorous Butterwort plant |url= https://www.cbsnews.com/news/nature-up-close-butterworts/ |website=[[CBS News]] |date= 14 June 2018 |access-date=29 December 2021}}</ref> This serves as a way for the plant to access a source of nitrogen, as they generally grow in soil that is acidic and low in nutrients, such as bogs.<ref name=CBSnews/><ref name=defenseplants>{{cite web |title= A Circumboreal butterwort |url= https://www.indefenseofplants.com/blog/2015/12/30/a-circumboreal-butterwort |website= In defense of plants |date= 30 December 2015 |access-date= 29 December 2021}}</ref> Insect capture is an adaptation to nutrient-poor conditions, and the plant is highly dependent on insects for nitrogen.<ref>{{cite journal | jstor=2434191 | last1=Karlsson | first1=P. S. | last2=Carlsson | first2=B. | title=Why does ''Pinguicula vulgaris ''L. trap insects? | journal=The New Phytologist | year=1984 | volume=97 | issue=1 | pages=25–30 | doi=10.1111/j.1469-8137.1984.tb04105.x | doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Distribution==
It has a generally [[Circumboreal Region|circumboreal distribution]], being native to almost every country in [[Europe]] as well as [[Russia]], [[Canada]], and the [[United States]].<ref name=defenseplants/><ref name=DVF>{{cite web |title=Den Virtuella Floran, ''Pinguicula vulgaris'' L. |first=Arne |last=Anderberg |publisher=Naturhistoriska riksmuseet, Stockholm, Sweden |url=http://linnaeus.nrm.se/flora/di/lentibularia/pingu/pingvulv.jpg }}</ref> It is generally found growing in places such as bogs, [[fen]]s, alvars, and other areas with limestone bedrock and alkaline waters.<ref name=defenseplants/>
